x.A: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so images could be lost if the AZ fails, which breaks the "cannot be lost" requirement.
x.B: One Zone-IA risks loss of images, and Flexible Retrieval after 360 days doesn't give instant availability on request.
x.C: Standard-IA keeps data across multiple AZs for the infrequent period, Glacier Instant Retrieval archives at 360 days with instant (millisecond) access, and Deep Archive after 5 years retrieves within 12 hours for auditors. It's the cheapest option that meets every requirement.
x.D: Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours, so images wouldn't be available instantly after 360 days.

x.A: A long-running cluster keeps paying for instances when the 6 hour job isn't running, which costs more than a transient cluster.
x.B: A transient cluster exists only for the 6 hour job. On-Demand primary and core nodes protect the data because core nodes store HDFS data, and Spot task nodes cut cost, since they don't hold data.
x.C: Core nodes hold data, so using Spot Instances for them risks data loss if they're interrupted.
x.D: A long-running cluster costs more, and Spot core nodes risk losing data.

x.A: An SCP can't require tags with values looked up from an RDS database, and it can't tag resources after the fact.
x.B: An EventBridge rule reacts to CloudTrail events when a resource is created, and a Lambda function looks up the creating user's cost center in the RDS database and tags the resource with it.
x.C: A scheduled rule can't invoke a CloudFormation stack in this way, and a schedule doesn't tag resources at creation using the creator's identity.
x.D: Tagging with a default value doesn't tag with the cost center ID of the user who created the resource.

x.A: Elastic Beanstalk with a single instance in a public subnet isn't highly available, and it still has the local Redis problem.
x.B: Lambda can't host a PHP application that serves static content and runs with this structure without a major rewrite.
x.C: Keeping the backend on a single EC2 instance leaves it as a single point of failure.
x.D: CloudFront with S3 serves the static content, an ALB with ECS on Fargate runs the PHP application with no servers to manage, and a Multi-AZ ElastiCache for Redis cluster holds sessions. Every tier is managed and highly available.

x.A: A public NLB works at layer 4, so it doesn't support AWS WAF or ALB-style cookie-based sticky sessions.
x.B: A Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting virtual appliances, not for exposing a web application.
x.C: A public ALB supports sticky sessions with cookies and integrates with AWS WAF, and it accepts the application target group.
x.D: A second target group with Elastic IPs doesn't create a load-balanced public endpoint with session affinity.
x.E: A WAF web ACL associated with the ALB endpoint filters malicious requests for additional security.

x.A: EBS with a web server on EC2 is more costly and not highly available across AZs.
x.B: EFS with EC2 costs more per GB than S3 and needs servers to manage.
x.C: S3 Standard is highly available, but each image is requested only once or twice a year, so Standard's higher storage price isn't the cheapest.
x.D: S3 Standard-IA is highly available across AZs and costs less per GB for rarely accessed images. With only one or two requests a year, retrieval fees are small, and a static website serves the images.

x.A: Security groups in the management account can't be used by other accounts' resources, because security groups are VPC-specific.
x.B: A customer managed prefix list holds the CIDRs, RAM shares it across the organization, and security groups reference the prefix list. Updating the list once updates the rules everywhere, at no extra cost.
x.C: AWS managed prefix lists are maintained by AWS for AWS services, so you can't put your own CIDRs in them.
x.D: Firewall Manager adds cost, and it's more than needed when a shared prefix list does the job.

x.A: A cluster placement group packs compute optimized instances close together in an AZ, which gives the lowest network latency between instances.
x.B: A partition placement group spreads instances across partitions for fault isolation, which doesn't minimize latency.
x.C: FSx for Lustre supports POSIX and not SMB, so it can't provide NFS and SMB multi-protocol access.
x.D: FSx for OpenZFS supports NFS only, not SMB, so it doesn't provide multi-protocol access.
x.E: FSx for NetApp ONTAP supports both NFS and SMB on the same data with low latency, so it meets the multi-protocol requirement.

x.A: DataSync would send the data over the VPN, which is 90% utilized, so it can't move 50 TB within 2 weeks.
x.B: Direct Connect takes weeks to provision, so it wouldn't be ready in time.
x.C: Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices hold 80 TB, are shipped to the data center, and securely transfer 50 TB offline within 2 weeks.
x.D: Storage Gateway moves data over the network, and the VPN doesn't have the spare bandwidth.

x.A: An ALB distributes traffic but doesn't add capacity before peak hours.
x.B: Memory isn't a default EC2 metric, and dynamic scaling still reacts after the load arrives.
x.C: Dynamic scaling on CPU reacts after the peak begins, so users still see slow performance until new instances are ready.
x.D: Peak hours occur at the same time each day, so scheduled scaling launches instances before peak begins, and the application performs well at the start.

x.A: DynamoDB is a different database and doesn't pool connections for RDS. The application would have to be rewritten.
x.B: RDS Proxy pools and shares connections to the database, so more application instances at peak times don't overload it. The applications only change the endpoint.
x.C: A custom proxy on EC2 means building and maintaining the proxy servers, which is more work.
x.D: A Lambda function isn't a connection pool for a database and adds code to maintain.

x.A: Monitoring with CloudWatch Logs and shrinking volumes takes effort, and EBS volumes can't be reduced in size with Elastic Volumes.
x.B: A custom script plus shrinking volumes is manual, and Elastic Volumes can only increase size, not decrease it.
x.C: Deleting expired and unused snapshots reduces cost but is a one-time manual cleanup, so the cost would grow again.
x.D: Deleting nonessential snapshots cuts the current cost, and Data Lifecycle Manager creates and deletes snapshots automatically by policy, so snapshot costs stay controlled with little effort.

x.A: KMS keys protect data at rest, but they don't restrict network access to RDS or limit who can reach the S3 bucket to the ECS cluster. The same key could also be used by anyone granted its permissions.
x.B: The AWS managed key encrypts the data but can't be restricted to the ECS role, and naming the task execution role as a user in the bucket policy doesn't limit RDS access.
x.C: The S3 bucket policy restricts bucket access to the ECS task execution role, and the RDS security group allows connections only from the subnets where the ECS tasks run. Together only the ECS cluster can reach the data in both services.
x.D: A security group limits RDS to the ECS subnets, but a bucket policy that allows the S3 VPC endpoint lets any resource in the VPC use the endpoint, not only the ECS cluster. It doesn't restrict S3 access to the ECS task role.

x.A: Burstable instances in unlimited mode can burst CPU well above the baseline when needed, which handles the 10x CPU surge. Scaling on request count adds instances as demand rises.
x.B: Compute optimized instances cost more all the time and aren't needed outside the two monthly surges.
x.C: Compute optimized instances scaled by schedule don't handle an immediate unpredictable surge, and cost more.
x.D: Elastic Beanstalk doesn't scale on predictive metrics the way the question describes, and scaling by requests is more direct.

x.A: Organizations manages accounts and governance, and it doesn't set up infrastructure.
x.B: CloudFormation provisions infrastructure as code, so setup is automated and repeatable, and Config records and audits every incremental change.
x.C: Organizations doesn't provision infrastructure, and Service Catalog doesn't track configuration changes.
x.D: CloudFormation is right, but Service Catalog manages approved products. It doesn't record changes to infrastructure.

x.A: A VPC has one internet gateway, and it's already highly available across AZs, so you don't provision one per AZ.
x.B: RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ keeps a standby in another AZ with automatic failover, so the database is highly available without changing the application.
x.C: Migrating to DynamoDB needs the application code to change, which isn't allowed.
x.D: DataSync copies files and isn't a database replication tool for a MySQL database.
x.E: An ALB with an Auto Scaling group across two AZs makes the stateless Python application highly available without code changes.

x.A: Gateway endpoints work only from within the VPC and can't be reached from on premises over Direct Connect.
x.B: A transit gateway connects networks and isn't a way to reach the S3 service privately.
x.C: Interface endpoints for S3 have private IP addresses in the VPC, which on-premises clients can reach over Direct Connect, so both the Region and on premises access S3 without the internet.
x.D: A KMS key encrypts data and doesn't control the network path.

x.A: An IAM policy can require that a tag be present but can't validate its value against a list of approved names across accounts.
x.B: A Deny policy on any resource with the tag does the opposite of the requirement.
x.C: Resource Groups can find and group resources by tag, but doesn't prevent resources from being created without approved values.
x.D: An Organizations tag policy defines the allowed values for the application name tag, so resources that don't follow the tag standard are flagged, and with enforcement enabled for supported services, non-compliant tagging is blocked.

x.A: A custom Lambda function on a schedule means writing and maintaining the rotation code.
x.B: Changing the password with the CLI is a manual step each time.
x.C: Secrets Manager integrates with RDS and rotates the master user password automatically on a schedule, such as every 30 days, with no custom code.
x.D: Parameter Store doesn't have native automatic rotation for RDS passwords.

x.A: On-demand mode costs more per request, and the company knows the load exactly, so it doesn't need to pay for flexibility.
x.B: Provisioned mode with the capacity set to the known load costs less than on-demand for predictable usage, and the capacity can be adjusted for the 4 hours of testing.
x.C: Reserved capacity needs a 1 year commitment, and the table is used only 4 hours a week, so it wouldn't be used enough to save money.
x.D: A 3 year reservation has the same issue and a longer commitment.

x.A: A zero spend budget alerts when any spend occurs, so it can't detect unusual spending in an account that already has normal spend.
x.B: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to find unusual spending and notifies stakeholders, with no thresholds to set.
x.C: Pricing Calculator estimates costs ahead of time and doesn't monitor actual spending.
x.D: CloudWatch doesn't monitor costs and detect unusual spend patterns for you.

x.A: A Spark catalog and Glue jobs require writing code and managing jobs, which is more effort for quick analysis.
x.B: A Glue crawler discovers the data's schema in S3, and Athena queries it with SQL right away, serverless and with no infrastructure.
x.C: Hive metastore tables and Spark jobs on EMR means running a cluster, which is more overhead.
x.D: Kinesis Data Analytics is for streaming data, not for ad hoc queries of files already in S3.

x.A: DataSync only copies data and doesn't give local SMB access with a cache for the files accessed often in the first 7 days.
x.B: An S3 File Gateway keeps recently accessed files cached locally for SMB access and stores them in S3. A lifecycle rule transitions data to Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days, with a retrieval time within 12 to 48 hours, which fits the 24 hour requirement with standard retrieval, at the lowest cost.
x.C: FSx File Gateway works with FSx for Windows File Server, not with S3 lifecycle transitions.
x.D: Giving each user S3 access changes how they use the file share and has no local cache for frequent access.

x.A: RDS doesn't auto scale the instance for read load. Storage autoscaling only grows disk space.
x.B: A read replica takes read traffic off the primary database, which is where the load is heavy.
x.C: The standby in a Multi-AZ deployment can't serve read traffic, so sending reads there doesn't work.
x.D: An ElastiCache cluster caches query results, so repeated reads don't hit the database, which reduces the heavy read load.
x.E: Placing instances in the same AZ as the database removes redundancy and doesn't fix read load.

x.A: A role that can delete snapshots on a new instance doesn't prevent accidental deletion by the storage administrator.
x.B: A deny policy attached to the storage administrator changes their administrative rights, which the question says not to do.
x.C: Recycle Bin retention rules keep deleted snapshots for recovery, but they don't prevent the deletion itself. The request asks to prevent deletion.
x.D: Snapshot lock prevents deletion of EBS snapshots for a set period, so accidental deletion can't happen even by administrators, without changing their permissions.
